Turning 71 this year? Your RRSP has to be closed by December 31: cash it out, buy an annuity, or transfer it to a RRIF.

Cash out: the whole amount is income that year, and on a lump sum over $15,000 the issuer withholds 30% (outside Québec). On $300,000 that's $90,000 withheld up front, and it isn't even the final tax. Annuity or RRIF: no tax is withheld on the direct transfer; you're taxed as the payments come in. The real danger is doing nothing: if the plan no longer qualifies as an RRSP, CRA treats you as having received the full value as income.

Take CPP at 60, or wait until 70? The difference is permanent.

Start before 65 and your CPP retirement pension is reduced by 0.6% for each month, up to 36% at 60. Wait past 65 and it grows 0.7% a month, up to 42% at 70. Example: if your pension would be $1,000 a month at 65, it's $640 at 60 and $1,420 at 70, more than double from 60 to 70.

Giving money or investments this Christmas? Canada has no gift tax, and a gift you receive isn't income. But some gifts can still cost the person who gives them.

1) Money you give your spouse or common-law partner to invest: the interest, dividends and capital gains are taxed to you (the attribution rules). Exception: money your spouse puts into their own TFSA isn't attributed back to you.

Down on a stock this year? In Canada, a capital loss can offset your capital gains, but only if the sale lands in the right year.

The rule: capital losses offset capital gains only (not your salary or other income).

Why December 30 (2026): Canadian trades settle one business day later (T+1), and CRA treats the settlement date as the date you sold. A trade on Wednesday, December 30 settles December 31; a December 31 trade settles in 2027. Confirm the cut-off with your broker.

The trap: if you or an affiliated person (like your spouse) buys the same stock within 30 days before or after the sale and still holds it 30 days later, it's a superficial loss and the loss is denied. It usually gets added to the cost of the shares bought back instead.

Losses inside a TFSA or RRSP can't be claimed at all.

Own an apartment back home or savings in a foreign bank? CRA may want Form T1135, even if you owe no tax.

Who files: Canadian residents whose specified foreign property cost more than $100,000 in total, at any time in the year. Under $250,000 all year → the simplified Part A; $250,000 or more → the detailed Part B.

Counts: money in foreign bank accounts, a rental property abroad, shares of foreign companies (U.S. stocks), even held at a Canadian broker.
Doesn't count: a vacation home you use mainly yourself, property used only in an active business, and anything inside an RRSP or TFSA.

Cost, not market value. For newcomers, the cost is the fair market value on the day you became resident.

The year you become resident: no T1135. The $100,000 test starts the next year. Your world income is still reported.

Late? The penalty is the greater of $100 or $25 a day, up to $2,500 (more if the failure is knowing). It's due with your return (April 30, or June 15 if you or your spouse run a business).

text:
Leaving Canada for good? CRA can tax your investments even if you never sell them. This is the departure tax (often called the exit tax).

The rule: when you become a non-resident, most property is treated as sold at fair market value on that day (and bought back at the same value). The gain is reported on Form T1243.

Example: shares outside an RRSP or TFSA bought for $40,000 and worth $100,000 when you leave → a $60,000 gain, and half of it, $30,000, is added to your income that year.

Not treated as sold: RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs and pension plans, and personal-use items worth under $10,000. Resident 60 months or less in the last 10 years? Property you owned when you arrived (or inherited after) is generally excluded, unless it's taxable Canadian property.

Paperwork: if everything you own is worth more than $25,000, list it on Form T1161. Can't pay? Form T1244 defers the tax, interest-free, until you sell; elect by April 30 of the year after you leave. Federal tax over $16,500 → CRA requires security.

When you become a non-resident depends on your ties to Canada. Plan with a professional before you go.
